title: What is known about 1RB---_1RC1RF_1LD1RA_1LB0LE_1LF1LF_0RB0LD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB---_1RC1RF_1LD1RA_1LB0LE_1LF1LF_0RB0LD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a base-4 counter whose digits are defects in a periodic background. Lean proves its rounds for all block lengths; the collisions of digits, which happen because the blocks between them run out at a critical rate, are only described empirically, and a tape of the same shape is proved to halt, so a proof has to follow the block lengths exactly.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (A1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 75,414 cells have been visited and 25,257 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.547). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: The counter's rounds
claims.text: Seven rounds from the head in state D at the left end to the next such moment, for all block lengths: the first digit going q→r (its block loses a period), r→s, p→q; a carry into the second digit (q, r or p); and the overflow of a one-digit counter into END, which creates a new first digit.

claims.title: A tape of the same shape halts
claims.text: From the tape 2<sup>4</sup> r 2<sup>2</sup> END (head in state D at the left end) the machine halts after 234,048 steps. The shape alone does not keep it running.

claims.title: The counter rule matches the run
claims.text: Of the 94,852 rounds in the first 10<sup>10</sup> steps the base-4 counter rule predicts 94,716 exactly and none wrongly; the other 136 are 31 overflows, 100 collisions of digits and 5 rounds of the first 120 steps. At most 8 digits.

claims.title: The four sweeps
claims.text: The pass to the right (state B) turns a block of the background into 1s; the pass back writes the background again in one of three phases, by its state: D writes 010, E writes 001, F writes 100. For all block lengths. The state of the pass back is how a carry (or its absence) travels to the left.

claims.title: No halt in the first 3.16·10<sup>15</sup> steps
claims.text: The macro simulator of the shared tools (blocks of 3 cells, whole runs of the background crossed at once; exact, tested cell for cell against the plain simulator) runs 3,162,277,665,785,965 steps (665,350,460 macro steps) without a halt.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.28×10<sup>19</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 12,898,417,544,340,449,177 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,030,112 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: What an overflow does to the blocks
claims.text: Between two overflows with the same digits and no collision, the block before END loses 1 period and the j-th block from the right loses 4<sup>j</sup> (1, 4, 16, 64, 256 at the overflows of steps 1.6·10<sup>7</sup> to 4.4·10<sup>7</sup>). The block before END went 8, 7, …, 1 and END then absorbed the last digit over six overflows (clusters 1,1,1 → 3,1 → 1,0,1 → 3 → 1,0 → 2 → 1), during which no new digit is made and the first block keeps growing; the next block before END went 42, 41, …, 29 by 10<sup>10</sup> steps and is at 9 after 3.16·10<sup>15</sup>.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. No halt in 3.16·1015 steps. Missing: the rules of every collision (the compound defects seen so far form a small set) and of END absorbing a digit, as local rules of the two passes, and an invariant on the block lengths that keeps the digits from wrecking END; the blocks are spent at a critical rate, so the invariant has to be exact. The next absorption of a digit by END (the block before it is at 9 and loses 1 per overflow) is due around 1016–1017 steps, within reach of py/far.py in a few hours.

check: python3 holdouts/1RB---_1RC1RF_1LD1RA_1LB0LE_1LF1LF_0RB0LD/py/counter.py 1e10   # the counter rule against the C simulator

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The machine counts in base 4 with digits written as defects in a periodic background, and the empty stretches between digits run out at exactly the rate that makes digits collide.

facts.text: its rounds proved in Lean for all block lengths.
rounds in 10<sup>10</sup> steps predicted exactly by the counter rule; the rest are overflows and collisions.
No halt in the C simulator; 75,414 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: A counter written in defects
html: Write down the gaps between consecutive 1s on the tape. Almost all of them are 2: the background is 001001001…. The exceptions are short defects of four kinds, q = (1,0), r = (4), s = (1,1) and p = (3), and the tape ends with a gap of 1 (END). Each time the head, in state D, is back at the left end, the tape is

and one round adds 1 to a base-4 counter whose digits are the defects, least significant first: q → r → s → p → q, with a carry on s → p. The head walks right only as far as the carry goes and comes back. The first block grows by one period every round, and each time a digit goes q → r the block after it loses one period.

When every digit is s, the carry runs to the end of the tape, comes back, and a new digit appears at the left end: the counter gains a digit at the bottom, and every old digit now turns over four times more slowly.

sections.heading: Blocks that run out on time
html: With K digits an overflow comes every 4K rounds. Right after one, the block behind the new digit is about 4K periods long, and it loses one period every four rounds, that is about 4K per cycle: it runs out just about when the next overflow comes. So blocks do reach zero, two digits touch, and the pair cycles as one compound defect until the two merge into one digit (pairs seen: rr → sr → ps → qs → pt → qt → p, and rq → sq → pr → qr → (6) → (1,3), which turns the carry back like the end of the tape).

Whether this goes on forever depends on the exact lengths. A tape of the very same shape, 24 r 22 END, halts after 234,048 steps (proved in Lean), when its digits drift into the end of the tape and destroy it. From blank tape the blocks have so far always been long enough; after 1010 steps the counter has 8 digits.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.547). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 75,414 cells (60,727 left of the start, 62 right), with a density of 1s of 0.335.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A base-4 counter written as defects in a 001 background, gaining a digit at the bottom on overflow; its blocks run out at a critical rate, so digits collide and merge (open; no halt in 3·10^15 steps).
